name: Anthracene Green
lede: Anthracene Green is a deep blue-green named for a coal-tar chemical, one of over a hundred color names that began on the chemist's bench.

sections.title: A name from the laboratory
sections.body:
Anthracene is a hydrocarbon from coal tar, and Paterson says any color made from it can carry its name, with anthracene red and green as examples [1]. Anthraquinone, a related compound, was used to manufacture alizarin, the coloring molecule of [[madder]] [1]. Garfield reports a count of 7,500 color names by an American standards body, of which over 100 came directly from synthetic dyes, anthracene green among them [2]. His other example is naphthalene yellow [2].

The books we hold do not describe the color anthracene green itself, so what it looked like in the 1800s is undocumented [1][2]. The swatch is Ridgway's 1912 plate 7 (hue 39), a dark blue-green, close to [[teal]] and [[myrtle-green]] [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this one covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 30, led by Henner's Alsatian Girl (1873), where it fills about a third of the picture [4]. It is also found in Kirchner's Two Girls under an Umbrella (1910) and Matisse's Music (1910) [4]. Three paintings before 1500 match, including a Memling of 1480, so the color was available long before the dye [4]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, and the match is not a pigment test [4].
